title: Luke 22
description: Luke 22 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 The Feast of Unleavened Bread,a which is called Passover, was approaching. 2 The lead priests and scripture scholars were looking for a way to do away with Jesus,b since they were afraid of the people. 3 The Adversaryc went into Judah,d the one called Ish-Kerioth,e who was one of the Twelve. 4 After leaving, he spoke with the lead priests and officers of the temple guard about how to hand him over to them. 5 They were overjoyed and arranged to give him money. 6 He agreed and began looking for an opportunity to hand him over to them away from the crowd.
7 Then the day came for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb was to be slaughtered. 8 Jesusf sent Peter and John,g saying, “Go prepare the Passoverh for us to eat.”
9 “Where do you want us to prepare it?” they asked him.

10 “Look, when you enter the city,” he told them, “Someonei will meet you, carrying a jug of water. Follow him into the house where he goes inside, 11 and tell the owner of the house, ‘The teacher says to you, “Where is the guest roomj where I may eat with my students?”’ 12 He will show you a large, furnished room upstairs. Prepare it there.” 13 When they went, they found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

14 And when the hour came, Jesusk took a seat at the tablel and the commissioned onesm did so with him. 15 He said to them, “I have longedn to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. 16 You see, I’m telling you, I won’t eat it until it is fully realizedo in God’s Reign.”

17 Then after picking up a cup and giving thanks, he said, “Take this and distribute it among yourselves 18 because, I’m telling you, from now on, I won’t drink any of what is produced by the vine until God’s Reign comes.”

19 Then after taking some bread and giving thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, given for your sake. Do this in remembrance of me.” 20 And likewise, after they ate the meal, he took the cup, saying, “This cup that is poured for your sake is the new covenant connected with my blood. 21 But look, the hand of the one who is handing me over is with me at the table. 22 After all, certainly the Son of Humanity is going according to what has been appointed, but how pitiable for that person by whom he is handed over!” 23 Then they began to explore together which of them might be about to do this.

24 There was also contentious rivalry among them about which of them seemed to be the most prominent. 25 So Jesus said to them, “The kings of other peoples lord it over them, and those who hold authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’p 26 But not so with you! Instead, the one who is most prominent among you must become like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves. 27 After all, who is more prominent, the one who is seated or the one who serves? Isn’t it the one who is seated? But I am among you as one who serves. 28 You are the ones who have continued to stay with me throughout my times of testing. 29 And I, in turn, pass down a Reign to you, just as my Father passed it down to me, 30 so you may eat and drink at my table in my Reign. You will sit on thrones governingq the twelve tribes of Israel.

31 “Simeon, Simeon,r pay attention! The Adversary has demanded to sifts yout like wheat, 32 but I have pleadedu for you so that your faithfulness won’t give out. When you return, support your Family members.”v
33 “Lord,” he said to Jesus,w “I am ready to go with you to prison and death!”
34 But Jesusx said, “I’m telling you, Peter, the rooster won’t crow today until you have disowned knowing me three times.”
35 Then he said to them, “When I sent you without a pouch of money or a sack of provisions or even sandals, you didn’t lack for anything, did you?”
“Nothing,” they said.

36 He told them, “But now, whoever has a pouch of money, take it along, and the same with a sack of provisions, and whoever doesn’t have a short swordy should sell their cloak and buy one. 37 You see,z I’m telling you that this scripture must be completedaa in connection with me: ‘And he was counted as being withbb people outside Torahcc.’dd After all, my part is reaching its completion.”ee
38 Then they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.”
“It is enough,”ff he told them.
39 After leaving, Jesusgg went, as usual, to the Mount of Olives, and the students followed him too. 40 When he came to the spot, he said to them, “Pray that you don’t come into a time of testing.”

41 He withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, and kneeling down, he prayed, 42 “Father, if you’re willing, take this cup away from me. However, let what you want happen, not what I want.” hh⟦ 43 Then a messenger from the heavens appeared to him, strengthening him.ii 44 Being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. ⟧jj

45 After getting up from prayer, when he came to the students, he found them asleep from grief. 46 “Why are you sleeping?” he said to them. “Get up and pray that you don’tkk come into a time of testing!”
47 While he was still speaking, suddenly a crowd was there, and the one named Judah, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He approached Jesus to kiss him.ll
48 “Judah,” Jesus said to him, “are you handing over the Son of Humanity with a kiss?”
49 At seeing what was happening, the others around him said, “Lord, should we strike them with swords?” 50 Then one of them struck the person enslaved to the high priest and severed his right ear.
51 “Allow this much!”mm Jesus responded, and he held the man’s ear and restored him.

52 Then Jesus said to the lead priests, officers of the temple guard, and elders who had moved against him, “Did you come out with swords and clubs as if against an armed outlaw? 53 Each day while I was with you in the sacred grounds, you didn’t stretch out your hands against me. But this is your time and the authority of darkness.”nn

54 Seizing him, they took him and brought him to the high priest’s house, but Peter began following at a distance. 55 After they made a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat among them.
56 After seeing him sitting in the firelight and looking intently at him, an enslaved womanoo said, “This man was with him too!”
57 But he denied it, saying, “Madam,pp I don’t know him.”
58 A short time later, someone else who saw him stated, “You are one of them too.”
But Peter stated, “Sir,qq I am not.”
59 After about an hour, another person started insisting, “This man was definitely with him too, because he’s also Galilean!”

60 But Peter said, “Sir, I don’t know what you’re talking about!” Right then, as he was still speaking, a rooster crowed. 61 And the Lord turned and looked right at Peter, and Peter remembered what the Lord had said, how he had told him, “You will disown me three times before the rooster crows today.” 62 Then he went outside and sobbed with grief.

63 The men who were holding Jesusrr began mocking and beating him. 64 After blindfolding him, they asked him repeatedly, “Prophesy! Who hit you?” 65 They kept saying many other things, heaping contemptss on him.

66 When daylight came, the elders of the people gathered, both the lead priests and the scripture scholars, and they led him away to their Sanhedrin.tt 67 They said, “If you are the Christ,uu tell us.”

But he told them, “If I say it to you, you certainly won’t trust it. 68 Yet if I ask, you certainly won’t answer. 69 From now on, the Son of Humanityvv will be seated at the right handww of the Power of God.”xx
70 They all said, “Then, are you the Son of God?”yy
So he told them, “You yourselves are saying that I am.”zz
71 “Why do we need any more testimony? After all, we heard it ourselves from his own mouth!” they said.

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: See Exodus 12:1–20 and Deuteronomy 16:1–8.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: The word satanas was not a name. It meant ‘adversary’ in the sense of prosecutor or opponent. It carries the meaning of someone who is against another, trying to sabotage their efforts and their wellbeing, and against someone as a plaintiff in court. It is an enemy, but also someone accusing another of wrongdoing, whether truly or falsely. It’s not just about pointing out something bad, but actively moving to cause adversity for someone else. The concept of Ha Shatan in the Hebrew Bible was not the evil archnemesis of God that Christian teaching has turned it into. It was described as a member of the council of spiritual beings whose role was to test people to see how genuine they were. The clearest example of this is in the book of Job.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Judas.’ Judas is the English version of the Greek version (Ioudas) of the Hebrew name Yehudah, or ‘Judah’ as it is typically rendered in English translations of the Hebrew Bible.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Iscariot.’ It was likely not his name, however. It means ‘man of Kerioth’ which was a city of Moab that was condemned for its actions against Israel, and it was likely used as a label regarding his betrayal of Jesus. See Jeremiah 48:21–47 (especially verses 21–27).

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: The name ‘John’ is the English version of the Latin version of the Greek transliteration (Ioannes) of the Hebrew name Yohanan or in English translations of the Hebrew Bible, Johanan, which means “God has been gracious” or “My God is gracious.”

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: The word is pascha for both Passover and the Passover lamb.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Many translations use ‘man’ here. The word is anthropos, which just means ‘person’ or ‘human.’ It is sometimes used for a man when distinguishing from a woman, but the usual term for that is aner. What does seem to indicate the person is a male is the pronouns. When a person’s gender is unspecified, Greek uses masculine pronouns, so the grammar leaves open the possibility of a man or woman, but Jesus seems to have someone in mind. In that case, if the person in mind were a woman, he would have used feminine pronouns. There is a common sermon point used about this verse that the strangeness of a man carrying the water was exactly the sign for the students to find the person easily; it does not hold up historically. While women were more frequently the ones responsible for carrying water, it was not so unheard of as the sermon tradition implies.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: This is the same word for ‘guest room’ as in Luke 2:7.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘reclined,’ which was the posture for eating a meal in the culture.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘apostles.’ The word means ‘someone who is sent to carry out a purpose’ and while it became used in a particular way in the church, it was not an inherently religious word in the Greek language.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: Literally, “I have desired with desire,” mirroring a Hebrew syntax that serves to emphasize intensity.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘fulfilled.’ It could be translated as something like ‘given a fuller meaning.’ It literally means ‘filled full.’ Much like ‘order fulfillment’ when purchasing an order to be delivered, it means to act on something and bring it to reality in a new way.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: The Greek word here is euergetes, literally “one who does good work.” It was not a description but an honorific bestowed as part of a formal arrangement. Ptolemaic kings and others used it as royal titles, and Greek cities voted to bestow it on the wealthy and powerful, which involved inscribing it in stone, often alongside soter (‘liberator’ or ‘savior’). The benefactor would be someone who donated some object or project or resource to the city. Since the honor of a title never equaled the value of the donation, the city was permanently indebted to the benefactor, owing loyalty and ongoing favors. Most often, the title was given to people who held power over the city in some way, so that the people could stay in the powerful person’s good graces. The especially relevant point for this passage is that the benefactors didn’t give themselves the title; it was bestowed by the people they dominated, binding the people to themselves through a show of generosity that left the people permanently in their debt, not truly being a generous gift at all.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The Greek here literally says ‘judging’ (krinontes). In biblical contexts, this does not indicate court proceedings and punishment but the role of the judges in the book of Judges. They were the leaders of the community, discerning how to keep the community thriving and protected.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: In English, repeating someone’s name twice can sound patronizing, but in the culture of the text, the repetition of a name in address is always a soft response, indicating compassion or pleading.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: Sifting was an idiom that indicated testing, with the image of determining what is genuine wheat grain and what is empty husk.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The word ‘you’ is plural, indicating not just Simeon but at least all twelve commissioned ones and maybe all the people present.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘prayed,’ but the word is more specific than any kind of prayer and isn’t exclusive to prayer. It is the verb for ‘be in need,’ ‘ask,’ or ‘beg,’ expressing strong need and the request to meet the need. It was used in many contexts, not just prayer to God.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: The word adelphos literally means ‘brother’ or ‘sibling.’ It was also frequently used to refer to ‘cousin’ or ‘relative,’ and even for members of the same ideological or ethnic group.

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: The word here is machaira, specifically referring to a short sword or large knife, part of the equipment ordinarily included for travel.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: The Greek word gar, traditionally translated as ‘for’ and here rendered as ‘you see’ indicates that what comes next is the reason for the instruction just given, the change from taking nothing with them to now being told to bring money, provisions, and swords.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Or ‘fulfilled’ or ‘performed’ in the sense of bringing about an end result pointed to by the writing.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: The quotation of Isaiah 53:12 here is different than the Septuagint Greek that it cites. The Septuagint reads en tois anomois, which means “among those outside Torah.” The Greek of Luke’s text here reads meta anomon, which is something closer to “with those outside Torah.” The preposition meta (‘with’) indicates accompaniment and is the same one used in verse 15 to indicate who would be his Passover companions. To refer to “those outside the Torah” or the ‘without-Torah’ ones would be a reference to Gentiles, people who had no connection with Torah or the Mosaic covenant. See the next footnote for more information.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: The Greek word nomos means ‘law,’ ‘custom,’ or ‘established norm.’ The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) used nomos to render torah, and the New Testament writers continued to use it with that sense in many places. It served as a Greek label for that body of writing rather than a rendering of what torah itself means, which is closer to ‘instruction’ or ‘direction.’ The word here is anomos (literally something like ‘no-law’ or, in this context, ‘no-torah’) and it is used in two ways across the New Testament. In one, it describes status: people outside the covenant community and therefore not under Torah, which would essentially be synonymous with ‘Gentile’ and not a statement about behavior. In the other, it describes people whose conduct is contrary to a moral standard, closer to ‘lawless.’ This verse is rendered as the first sense, based in part on how the word is used by the same biblical writer (Luke) in Acts 2:23.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: Quotation of Isaiah 53:12

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: The Greek phrase telos echei literally reads ‘has an end’ and is an idiom for being at an end or reaching the end. The root is the same as telesthēnai earlier in this verse, translated as ‘be completed.’ It can carry the sense of arriving at an intended goal or simply stopping. Both are likely meant here: what has been written about him arrives at its goal at the same time that he arrives at the end of his work and life. The subject in this sentence, to peri emou, is literally ‘the thing concerning me,’ which is what is rendered here as ‘my part.’

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: The Greek hikanon estin literally means ‘it is enough’ or ‘it is sufficient.’ Many scholars interpret it as Jesus cutting off the conversation because he is exasperated that they misunderstood him. Though it’s possible, there is no grammatical indication, such as an imperative, that this is what is happening. In contrast, later in this chapter, in verse 51, the grammar does include an imperative when he stops one of his followers from using a sword against someone. This verse seems simply to be the natural end of an exchange, with Jesus responding to what they said. The confusion happens because Jesus’ followers respond to the part about a packing list for travel, but don’t acknowledge the Isaiah quotation. The reversal of the earlier instruction not to bring supplies is based on that quotation as applied to Jesus, and specifically how Jesus is counted as being with (seemingly as a companion) people outside Torah, i.e. Gentiles. What Jesus imagines they will do with the swords is debated, but whatever it is, later in this chapter, Jesus prevents them from using them for armed resistance.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Luke 22:43–44 is a contested passage, appearing inconsistently among the earliest sources available. Many of the most reliable and earliest manuscripts don’t include it (including Papyrus 75, which is estimated to have been made about 200 CE), and many other early and reliable manuscripts do include it. Patristic writings make reference to it, including Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho and Irenaeus’ Against Heresies. This translation follows the SBL Greek New Testament, which includes it. The early usage of the passage is relevant for interpreting the significance of it today. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus’ use of it was to argue for the embodiment of Jesus, that he was a real human and not a divine manifestation that only seemed human (a view known as Docetism). The physical vulnerability, the sweat and exhaustion, were presented as the proof. In the late fourth century, Epiphanius of Salamis asserted that the verses were removed by scribes who found them troubling. Others have argued that it was added to provide support for arguments against Docetism. Either way, vulnerability is an essential part of Jesus’ story, and it has always made people uncomfortable, perhaps even to the point of removing it from the text.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: The Greek word translated as “strengthening him” appears in the Septuagint version of Daniel 10:19 (showing up in the final clause of the following quotation). It is in the context of Daniel in conversation with a heavenly messenger. It reads: Again one in human form touched me and strengthened me. He said, “Do not fear, greatly beloved; you are safe. Be strong and courageous!” When he spoke to me, I was strengthened and said, “Let my lord speak, for you have strengthened me” (Daniel 10:18–19 NRSVue).

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: See note at the beginning of verse 43.

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: Or “pray so you don’t”

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: The word is phileo, which literally means ‘love’ or ‘have affection for’ or ‘be attached to’ and can also be used to mean ‘kiss’ as a way to demonstrate affection (though not only romantic or sexual affection as in American culture, but also in friendship or familial affection). It was a common cultural practice for students to kiss their teachers in greeting.

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: The Greek phrase here, eate heos toutou, appears nowhere else in the New Testament and may be unique in all Greek literature. It is a compressed phrase that leaves some of the meaning implicit, and its sense has to be worked out from context. The verb eate is plural and carries two basic meanings: permit and leave alone. The phrase heos toutou means “up to this point” or “this much”; it is uncommon in Greek but does appear in the Septuagint, in Exodus 7:16 and Leviticus 26:18. Most modern English translations render it with the ‘leave alone’ meaning of the verb, along the lines of “No more of this.” This translation renders it with the ‘permit’ meaning. The first one shows Jesus wants the swords to stop, but this translation addresses why the swords should stop: because what is happening is being allowed, just as Jesus prayed, saying, “Father, if you’re willing, take this cup away from me. However, let what you want happen, not what I want” in verse 42. This was the standard English rendering for nearly four centuries. Tyndale translated it as “Soffre ye thus farre forthe” (“suffer ye thus far forth”) in 1534, and subsequent translations kept that interpretation through the Geneva Bible, the King James Version, the American Standard Version and others through the 1920s before the tradition changed with the RSV in 1946 to “No more of this!” A comment preserved in the Greek catena on John, attributed to Apollinaris, calls the line a concession and observes that the word “up to” sets a limit and a check on the sword, reading it as the boundary of Jesus’ concession on swords in verses 36–38. The Gospel of John also makes the connection between the sword and the cup in John 18:11.

footnotes.label: nn
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 1:79 and Colossians 1:13.

footnotes.label: oo
footnotes.html: While most literally it means ‘girl’ this word (paidiske) was also used for enslaved women. ‘Woman’ is used here based on Peter’s address of the person with gunai in verse 57; it refers to an adult woman, not a child.

footnotes.label: pp
footnotes.html: Literally, the word means ‘woman.’ However, addressing a woman as ‘woman’ in our culture is considered rude, an attempt to put her in her place, especially when done by a man. In the culture of the time, it was a polite way to address someone.

footnotes.label: qq
footnotes.html: The word here is anthrope, literally meaning ‘human’ or ‘person.’ It is the masculine equivalent to gunai as ‘woman’ or ‘madam’ in verse 57. It is a polite address for a male stranger, but it is not deferential like kurios or epistates.

footnotes.label: rr
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: ss
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘blasphemously’ or ‘insulting’ from the Greek word blasphemeo. The Greek word means ‘revile,’ ‘defame,’ or ‘belittle.’

footnotes.label: tt
footnotes.html: Literally, it says ‘their sunedrion’ referring to a council, but based on the people who comprise it, it may refer to the council traditionally called the Sanhedrin in English from the same Greek word. Though there is scholarly debate about the historical reality, the tradition of the Mishnah is that the Sanhedrin was the highest Judean judicial and council body, handling religious, civil, and criminal cases.

footnotes.label: uu
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew meshiah which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: vv
footnotes.html: Reference to Daniel 7:13–14

footnotes.label: ww
footnotes.html: Reference to Psalm 110:1

footnotes.label: xx
footnotes.html: The word dunamis literally means ‘power’ or ‘ability.’ It is sometimes used in place of referring to God directly, as was often the customary practice of the time. In Mark 14:62, it has this phrase without “of God” following. Luke seems to reference the same statement by Jesus but likely added “of God” for clarity for his non-Jewish audience.

footnotes.label: yy
footnotes.html: “The Son of God” was a nickname for the emperor, a title taken on originally by Augustus Caesar, the son of Julius Caesar who was worshiped as divine, and was then used by other, subsequent emperors.

footnotes.label: zz
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 4:41, where demons are the ones naming him as Christ and Son of God.
